# Semantic Validation with LLMs {#sec-semantic-validation}

```{python}
#| include: false
import pointblank as pb
import polars as pl
pb.config(report_incl_header=False, report_incl_footer=False)
```


Some expectations are hard to write as code. Whether a product review is a real, on-topic comment
is a judgment about meaning, and no regular expression or set membership check can make it. The
`prompt()` method handles cases like this. It sends each row to a language model along with a plain
description of what a good row looks like, and turns the model's answer into an ordinary pass or
fail test unit that appears in the report next to your other checks.

This comes with costs that regular checks do not have. Each check costs money, takes much longer to
run, and may not give exactly the same answer twice. So semantic validation is something to use on
purpose, not by default. This chapter covers how the method works, how to write prompts that give
reliable answers, how to include reference material as attachments, how to manage the cost, and how
the results fit into the rest of a validation plan. We use a small table of product reviews for the
examples.

```{python}
reviews = pl.DataFrame({
    "review_id": [1, 2, 3, 4],
    "product": ["wireless mouse", "desk lamp", "coffee mug", "usb cable"],
    "review_text": [
        "Works great, very responsive and comfortable to use all day.",
        "asdkjfh lorem ipsum dolor sit amet",
        "The lamp is bright and the base is sturdy. Very happy with it.",
        "n/a",
    ],
})

pb.preview(reviews, n_head=4, n_tail=0)
```
